evidence.title: Performance evaluation of large language models in pediatric nephrology clinical decision support: a comprehensive assessment
evidence.outcome: Hallucination occurrences in LLM answers to pediatric nephrology cases
evidence.quote: All models exhibited hallucinations (2-8 occurrences) and potentially life-threatening decisions (0-2 occurrences).

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether governance policies on incorrect, falsified, outdated, or unverifiable generative AI output reduce the harm from such output, and the support for this recommendation rests on one guidance document and two commentaries. One offline study found that every language model it examined produced hallucinations (2 to 8 occurrences) across 10 pediatric nephrology cases, which shows the problem exists but does not show that a policy addresses it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice. The single hazard study is a level 4 simulation of 10 clinical cases in France, so it is indirect, small, and offline. Endorsements come from one guidance document and two commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, certainty that governance policies change outcomes cannot be rated because no direct test exists.

All models in the pediatric nephrology simulation produced hallucinations, ranging from 2 to 8 occurrences across 10 cases. This suggests that incorrect generated content may reach clinicians if no check is in place. The study did not examine whether any institutional rule, review step, or verification requirement would catch these errors before they affect care.

The guidance source states that health care organizations should develop governance policies covering incorrect or falsified responses and the inability to verify sources. The two commentaries call for accountability frameworks and mechanisms to limit misinformation. These statements express expert expectation, and none of them reports a test of how such policies perform once adopted.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units with and without written policies on inaccurate generative AI output and measure error detection rates, errors reaching patients, clinician verification behavior, and the time and staff cost of policy compliance in live clinical workflows.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study used 10 simulated pediatric nephrology cases in France without reporting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore says nothing about whether such policies would work for these groups, who may face added risk if hallucinated content appears in translated or simplified patient materials.
